title: Solvenn Mutual: the discount for safe drivers
prompt: A motor insurer's economics are simple to write down and hard to run: it collects a premium, pays out claims, and carries the cost of selling and administering the policy. What is left is underwriting profit. Our client is Solvenn Mutual, which has one million motor policies and has priced them for decades on broad categories — age, address, vehicle — rather than on how anyone actually drives. Competitors now offer a telematics product: a phone app that measures braking, speed and mileage, gives the driver feedback, and rewards them with a discount. Solvenn's board wants to launch its own version, offering a discount on the premium to any policyholder who installs the app, and expects about a fifth of the book to take it up. Two things will matter today: the discount is paid to everyone who adopts, whether or not their driving changes, and the drivers who volunteer for an app that watches them are not a random sample of the book.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — How a motor policy makes money
exhibits.text: Premium collected − claims paid − expenses of selling and administering the policy = underwriting profit per policy. A discount reduces the premium on day one and for certain; a change in driving behaviour reduces claims later and only if it happens. Solvenn's board is being asked to trade one for the other.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Solvenn's motor book and the expected adopters (Scenario 1)

rows: Average annual claims cost before the app (USD)
Expected reduction in claims cost from app feedback

exhibits.unitsNote: Adopters are a subset of the book, not an addition to it. Their claims cost is measured before the app is installed; the 15% reduction applies to that figure. Expenses are unchanged by the app.
exhibits.source: Solvenn actuarial pack and the competitor trial published last year

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Scenario 2: the adopter group re-measured

rows: Average annual claims cost before the app (USD)
Expected reduction in claims cost from app feedback

exhibits.unitsNote: Changed from Scenario 1: the adopters' claims cost before the app is $400, not $480 — a closer look at who signed up for the competitor's product shows they are safer still. Every other figure is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Let's start with the right structure. What are the three key questions you would need to answer in order to tell Solvenn whether to launch the telematics discount? Please summarise them in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: Who adopts, and what do their claims look like before the app — are they already the book's safest drivers?
How much does the app actually change behaviour, and what is that worth against the discount Solvenn gives away to get it?
What does it do to the rest of the book — retention of the safest drivers, and the risk mix left behind if they leave.
commonMistakes: Reciting a generic pricing framework instead of the three questions this launch turns on.
Treating adopters as a random slice of the book, which is the assumption the whole case attacks.
Framing it only as a claims question and forgetting the discount is a certain cost.
Naming six things when the interviewer asked for three.

questions.followUp: Good. The actuarial team has put numbers to the launch, using the adoption profile seen in a competitor's product.

questions.prompt: Scenario 1: given the data in the exhibit, what would launching the telematics discount do to Solvenn's annual underwriting profit? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working. If profit falls, enter the answer with a minus sign, for example -250000.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Work per adopting policy, since nothing changes for the rest of the book.
Claims saved: the adopters' claims cost before the app is $480 — not the book average of $560 — and the app takes 15% off it: $480 × 15% = $72 a policy.
Discount given: 8% of the $800 premium = $64 a policy, paid to every adopter.
Net per adopting policy = $72 − $64 = $8.
Across 200,000 adopters: 200,000 × $8 = $1,600,000 a year.
Expenses are unchanged, and the 800,000 non-adopting policies are unaffected.
keyPoints: The saving applies to the adopters' own claims cost, which is well below the book average — that is the selection effect.
The discount is certain and universal among adopters; the saving is a percentage of a smaller base.
Only the adopting policies are in the calculation at all.
commonMistakes: Using the book-average claims cost of $560 and answering 200,000 × ($84 − $64) = $4,000,000 — the single most common error here.
Applying the discount to the whole book of one million policies and answering a large negative number.
Netting the 15% against the 8% as if they were percentages of the same base.
Including expenses, which the app does not change.

questions.prompt: Please explain briefly the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question, in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: Only adopters are affected, so the whole calculation is per adopting policy times the number of adopters.
The claims saving is 15% of the adopters' own claims cost, and adopters are already safer than the book, so the base is $480 rather than $560.
The discount is 8% of the full premium, given to every adopter whether or not their driving changes.
The two nearly cancel: the margin is $8 a policy, which is thin enough that any error in either input matters.
commonMistakes: Explaining the arithmetic without naming the selection effect that sets the base.
Describing the discount as a cost of acquisition rather than a reduction in premium already being collected.
Not commenting on how thin the resulting margin is.

questions.followUp: Understood. The actuarial team confirms the 15% figure is measured on adopters' own claims experience, before and after installation, in the competitor's published trial.

questions.prompt: I'd like to check a couple of the parameters behind that. In Scenario 1, how much would the app save in claims on a single adopting policy in a year? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per policy per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
An adopter's claims cost before the app is $480 a year.
The app reduces it by 15%: $480 × 0.15 = $72 a year.
keyPoints: The reduction applies to the adopter's claims cost, not to the book average and not to the premium.
commonMistakes: $560 × 15% = $84, using the book average.
$800 × 15% = $120, applying the reduction to the premium.
Answering $408, the claims cost after the reduction rather than the saving.

questions.followUp: Thanks. Note that the discount is set in the product terms and does not vary by driver: every adopter receives the same percentage off.

questions.prompt: And what would the discount cost Solvenn in total across all adopters in a year? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Discount per adopting policy = 8% × $800 = $64.
Across 200,000 adopters: 200,000 × $64 = $12,800,000 a year of premium given up.
keyPoints: The discount is a reduction in premium Solvenn is collecting today, so it is a real and immediate cost.
It is paid on every adopting policy, regardless of whether that driver's behaviour changes.
commonMistakes: Applying the discount to the whole book and answering $64,000,000.
Discounting the underwriting profit rather than the premium.
Netting the claims saving off before answering — the question asks for the discount alone.

questions.followUp: That gives the board both halves of the trade. Before we conclude, they want to know how sensitive the answer is.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements, if true, would change the annual profit impact you calculated? Select all that apply.
options: Running the app and processing its data would cost Solvenn $6 per adopting policy per year
Solvenn's regulator would require the discount to be offered to any policyholder who asks for it, though only the 200,000 adopters would install the app
Two competitors already sell a telematics product in this market
Claims costs across the market are expected to inflate by 5% next year, with premiums held flat
Adopters' claims cost before the app is $480 against a book average of $560

optionRationale: Changes it. $6 × 200,000 = $1.2M of running cost against an $8-a-policy margin, cutting the impact from $1.6M to $400,000. On a margin this thin, the cost of running the programme is not a rounding error.

Changes it, and it destroys the case. The discount would go to all one million policies — $64M of premium given up — while the claims saving stays with the 200,000 who install: $14.4M against $64M, an impact of −$49.6M. The discount and the behaviour change have to be tied to the same population.
Does not change it. Competitors matter for adoption rates and for retention, but neither the discount nor the claims saving in your calculation moves because a rival is in the market.

Changes it, and in Solvenn's favour. The saving is 15% of a claims cost that is now $504, worth $75.60 a policy, while the $64 discount is fixed to a premium that has not moved: the impact rises to $2.32M. Claims inflation makes claims-reducing programmes more valuable, not less.
Does not change it. That is the exhibit restated, and it is already the base you used.
keyPoints: Ask which term each statement touches: the population discounted, the population whose claims change, the base, or the rate.
The most dangerous statement is the one that breaks the link between who pays and who benefits.
A thin margin is sensitive to running costs that would be immaterial elsewhere.
commonMistakes: Picking the competitors' presence because it is strategically important, though it is not in this arithmetic.
Missing the regulator's requirement because it sounds procedural rather than economic.
Assuming claims inflation must hurt an insurer, without asking what it does to a saving expressed as a percentage.

questions.followUp: That is exactly the sensitivity the board was worried about. And the actuarial team has now looked harder at who actually signs up for products like this.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is likely to be true for Scenario 2 compared with Scenario 1? Use the data below for your revised calculation. The change is described under the exhibit.
options: The launch adds more profit in Scenario 2, because adopters are safer drivers
The launch now reduces Solvenn's underwriting profit
The profit impact is unchanged, because the discount and the claims reduction are both unchanged
There is not enough information to decide

optionRationale: Wrong, and it is the intuitive answer: safer adopters do cost less to insure, but Solvenn is not choosing whether to insure them — it already does. What it is choosing is whether to hand them 8% of their premium.

Correct. The saving is 15% of $400 = $60 a policy, against an unchanged $64 discount: −$4 a policy, or −$800,000 a year across 200,000 adopters. The safer the adopter, the less there is to save, while the discount stays the same — so the programme turns from value-creating to value-destroying.
Wrong. Both percentages are unchanged; what changed is the base the claims percentage applies to, which is the only thing that mattered.
Wrong. The adopters' claims cost, the reduction, the discount and the number of adopters are all given. Worth choosing where something is genuinely missing; here nothing is.
keyPoints: +$1.6M becomes −$800,000 on a single row of the exhibit.
A percentage discount on premium is fixed; a percentage saving on claims shrinks with the claims base.
Break-even is where 15% of the adopters' claims cost equals $64, that is a claims cost of about $427.
commonMistakes: Reading 'safer drivers' as 'better for the insurer' and choosing the first option.
Recomputing the whole book rather than the 200,000 adopters.
Choosing 'not enough information' because the re-measurement feels like it should come with more detail.

questions.prompt: Please explain in 2 to 3 lines the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question — and say what it implies about how Solvenn should design the discount.

keyPoints: The discount is a fixed percentage of premium; the saving is a percentage of a claims cost that falls as the adopter group gets safer.
So the better the drivers who self-select into the product, the worse the economics — which is the opposite of the board's instinct.

Design implication: tie the discount to the claims saved rather than to the premium, or vary it by the driver's measured score so that safe drivers who were never going to crash are not paid for behaviour they have not changed.
A strong answer also notes the defensive argument: Solvenn may have to launch anyway to stop competitors taking its safest drivers, and that is a retention case, not this one.
commonMistakes: Restating the numbers without drawing out the design implication the question asks for.
Concluding that Solvenn should avoid safe drivers, rather than that it should price the discount differently.
Ignoring the competitive reason the board wants to launch at all.

questions.followUp: That is the argument the board needs. Separately, the technology committee has asked whether Solvenn should build the app itself rather than license one.

questions.prompt: Choose the four pieces of data that, when combined, would allow us to estimate the net benefit to Solvenn of building its own telematics app, over the app's whole life.
options: Upfront cost to build, test and certify the app
Number of years the app will stay competitive before it must be rebuilt
Policies enrolled in each year of the app's life
Net benefit per enrolled policy — claims saved less discount given — in each year of the app's life
Cost of running the app and processing its data in each year of the app's life
The licensor's annual fee for the app Solvenn would otherwise buy
The average premium of an enrolled policy

optionRationale: Needed. Lifetime net benefit is what the app delivers less what it cost to build.
Not needed. Three of the other items are already given 'in each year of the app's life', so the number of years is carried by them.
Needed. Enrolment is what the per-policy benefit is applied to, and it will build over time.
Needed, and per year: the claims saving and the discount can both move as the book and the market change.
Needed. Running an app and processing driving data is an annual cost, not a one-off.
Not needed for this estimate. The licence fee is what you compare the answer with once you have it, not an input to the build's own benefit.

Not needed, and it is the easiest one to take by reflex, because the discount is a percentage of premium. But the net benefit per enrolled policy is already stated net of that discount — taking the premium as well would be counting the same thing twice.
keyPoints: Lifetime net benefit = Σ over years of (policies enrolled × net benefit per policy − running cost) − upfront cost.
That expression consumes exactly the four selected items and nothing else.
The price of the alternative is a comparison, not an input.
commonMistakes: Taking the number of years because a lifetime calculation obviously needs one, without noticing the per-year projections already carry it.
Taking the licensor's fee because the decision is build-versus-buy.
Taking the average premium because the discount is expressed as a percentage of it, when the per-policy benefit already nets the discount off.

questions.followUp: Thanks. One last thing before the board paper goes out.

questions.prompt: Your BCG project leader has asked you for the potential downsides of Solvenn launching the telematics discount — the things that could go wrong even if the arithmetic works. Could you share your thoughts in 3 to 4 lines?

keyPoints: The book left behind: if the safest fifth take a discount and everyone else stays, the average risk of the non-adopting book rises and its pricing is now wrong.
The measured 15% may not survive contact with a full launch — trial participants are the most motivated, and behaviour change decays once the novelty passes.
Adoption could be much higher or much lower than a fifth, and the economics are thin enough that either would matter.
Data, privacy and conduct risk: continuous location data on a million drivers, and a regulator that will ask how the discount is justified per customer.
Competitive response: rivals can match the discount, leaving Solvenn with the cost and none of the retention benefit that motivated the launch.
commonMistakes: Listing generic product-launch risks with no link to how the insurer earns money.
Missing the effect on the rest of the book, which is the risk specific to selective discounting.
Repeating the selection argument from earlier questions rather than naming new risks.

closing: That is everything. You held the discount and the claims saving to the same population, noticed that the saving rests on a smaller base than the book average, and then watched a single re-measurement of who adopts turn the launch from value-creating to value-destroying. Thank you — the board meets on Wednesday.
